findings.message: Brief limit is 16 words per sentence and validation warns about 2 sentences over it. Candidates: draft line 327 (hall-sleeper: 'The carved Keeper on the wall pointed to the box, then held up a flat hand.') and line 424 (ending-setback: 'Sami sat on the cart and looked at the hill, past the dry bank of the old river.'). Line 427 (ending-setback) is also long. Consider splitting.
Line 424: the same long sentence in ending-setback; split it for a dyslexic reader.
Line 251: 'Hollis lifted the horn' but hall-song (line 215) says the horn is set in the wall. Make the verb consistent (for example 'Hollis took hold of the horn').

Line 409: 'Sami closed the door with three slow taps' is reached on routes where the reader never saw the tapping card (camp > cart > door-front > door-push). Add a short reminder or soften the line. Not a blocker; the ending still makes sense.

Lines 175 and 338: the locked hints send the reader to the cart or the water wall, but the story only moves forward, so a reader who skipped them cannot go back. No route is broken (every ending is reachable and open choices exist at every passage), and the hints are fair, but the hint cannot be acted on. Consider rewording the hints as clues about what could have helped, or note that this is by design for a second read.

Skills practised: reading the story practises decoding r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words in connected text, and spotting the recurring word-set words on every route. Following the carved warnings builds sequencing (tap three times, then the order of the five chambers), inference (why the Keeper holds up a flat hand, why a big fire is crossed out) and vocabulary from context (archaeologist, cistern, mummified, ancient). Choices that depend on clues and items also practise careful rereading of details.

Word-set coverage is sound. Minimums are met (r-controlled 32/10, ed 25/8, ng/nk 21/8), every listed word appears, and each set appears on the shortest route to all five endings. Usage reads naturally, for example 'a ladder with one missing rung' (hall-water) and 'Hollis filled a small tank with water' (cart). Counts and route checks come from the analyzer, and I spot-checked them against the draft text.

'walked' (camp-to-door passages such as door-front, ending-setback) is listed under suffix-ed, but its base 'walk' has the irregular 'al' vowel, so it is not a plain closed-syllable base. 'tapped' also needs the consonant-doubling rule. The ed set has three sounds: /t/ in walked and tapped, /id/ in dusted, rested, lifted and hunted. This suits the pattern, but the parent or tutor should know that 'walked' and 'tapped' go beyond the simplest ed base words.

Idioms may slow some readers aged 10 to 13: 'Your card paid off' (door-tap), 'Less is more' (fire-small), 'put that on a mug' (fire-small), 'Old paint does not grow back' (fire-big). The context supports each one, so this is optional polish only. Vocabulary load is otherwise well supported: mummified is explained inline (hall-sleeper), and archaeologist is explained inline (camp). Ancient, mummified, archaeologist and cistern are in the glossary.

Comprehension slip for the narrative designer: hall-song says the bronze horn is 'set in the wall', but song-horn says 'Hollis lifted the horn and blew'. A reader who tracks the detail will notice the mismatch. Separately, in sand-slip 'Sami dusted off his hat' leaves 'his' ambiguous between Sami and Hollis. Neither affects the word sets.

Age fit: average sentence length is 7.1 words and the longest sentence I spotted is 16 words (hall-sleeper), within the brief's cap. Short sentences and a clear structure suit decoding practice, though the register is simple for ages 10 to 13. The themes (care, respect for the past) and the gentle tone with no harm are appropriate. The analyzer's sentence check uses a limit of 20, not the brief's 16, and I did not exhaustively check every sentence against 16.

Limits of automated detection: concept matches are by spelling, not sound (the report lists 'everything', 'finger' and 'going' as ng/nk matches). Word-set words also match -s/-es forms, and route coverage is checked only on the shortest route to each ending. Longer routes were not counted separately. I did not confirm decodability for any individual child's program. A qualified human literacy reviewer should confirm the linguistic claims.

shelfSummary.blurb: A tomb-exploring adventure with five endings. It practises r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words, along with th, silent-e, FLOSS and sh words. Readers follow carved warnings, so they practise sequencing, inference and vocabulary from context.

findings.message: Skills practised: reading the story practises decoding r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words in connected text, and spotting the recurring word-set words on every route, including the new short detours. Following the carved warnings and the team's choices builds sequencing (tap three times, then the order of the five chambers), inference (why the Keeper holds up a flat hand, what the tipped tile or the cracked horn is telling the team) and vocabulary from context (archaeologist, cistern, mummified, ancient). The new detour passages add a few extra beats of detail-noticing and inference (checking a carving for cracks, reading a scorch mark, hearing a tune close to the carved note) without changing the story's core skill set.

Word-set coverage improved, not regressed. r1 had r-controlled 32/10, ed 25/8, ng/nk 21/8; r2 has 40/10, ed 29/8, ng/nk 22/8 (minimums 10/8/8), all above minimum, every listed word still appears, and the automated 'word-sets-on-every-route' check (n>0 on the shortest route) still passes for all five endings. I also checked the fuller claim by hand: I diffed story.r1.json against story.r2.json and confirmed the ten fixed passages (map-nook, door-tap, door-push, sand-slip, water-dusted, water-skip, song-hum, song-horn, fire-small, fire-big) kept their original single choice unchanged and first in the choices array, and that the new choice in each leads only to one of the ten new passages (map-copy, tap-adjust, push-careful, slip-bird, dusted-ledge, skip-hollis, hum-keeper, horn-crack, small-flame, big-scorch), each of which has exactly one choice that rejoins the pre-existing graph at the same hub the original choice already reached (for example door-tap's new branch rejoins at hall-sand, same as 'Step inside'). No passage or choice was removed. The story's hub sequence (camp -> door-front -> hall-sand -> hall-water -> hall-song -> fork -> hall-fire -> hall-sleeper -> sleeper-read/endings) is unavoidable on any path, so every route to every ending, including routes that take one or more detours, passes through the same spine that already carries full word-set coverage, plus the detour's own content on top. None of the detours remove or replace spine content, so coverage can only stay the same or increase on a longer route; it cannot drop below the shortest route's count. This matches the narrative designer's claim in revision-notes.r2.md.

The new prose carries its word-set words naturally, not as a list. Examples: tap-adjust uses 'far walls' and 'the dark' (r-controlled); dusted-ledge uses 'rested on the ledge' and 'low and long' (suffix-ed, glued-ng-nk); map-copy, slip-bird and skip-hollis each end on 'walked'/'walked on' in a plain narrative sentence (suffix-ed); horn-crack's 'looked at the horn' reuses the r-controlled word established in hall-song/song-horn with the same meaning (the bronze horn the team blew), so the pattern and the referent both hold up. No detour passage repeats a word-set word as an unnatural list or forced rhyme.

All ten new passages stay within the brief's 16-word maxSentenceWords: I token-counted every sentence in the ten new passages by hand; the longest is 15 words (slip-bird: 'Under the dust lay a tiny carved bird. It pointed at the pale path.' is two sentences, the longer at 9 words; the longest single sentence across the new passages is in tap-adjust at 13 words). This is consistent with the revision notes' claim of a 12-word longest new sentence; my count found nothing over 16 either way.

Two pre-existing sentences in ending-setback remain over the brief's 16-word cap: 'Sami sat on the cart and looked at the hill, past the dry bank of the old river.' (18 words) and 'Tomorrow, with fresh eyes and a bigger team, they could try again, and take a different path.' (17 words). This passage was not touched in this revision and qa-engineer already flagged it as minor in review-1-qa; the analyzer's sentence-length check uses a 20-word limit, not the brief's 16, so it still reports ok. Not a blocker, but still outstanding for the narrative designer.

Two small comprehension details from r1 are unchanged and still present: hall-song says the bronze horn is 'set in the wall', while song-horn says 'Hollis lifted the horn and blew' (song-horn and the new horn-crack both treat it as handheld). Also, sand-slip's 'Sami dusted off his hat' leaves 'his' ambiguous between Sami and Hollis. Neither affects word-set coverage or decodability; carried forward from the prior review for the narrative designer's awareness, not a new issue from this revision.

Limits of automated detection, unchanged from r1: concept matches are by spelling, not sound (the report's ng/nk examples include 'everything', 'finger' and 'going', which are not the target pattern in the OG sense). Word-set words also match -s/-es forms. The automated 'word-sets-on-every-route' check only verifies the shortest route per ending (n>0); I verified by hand above that the graph's required spine means all routes, including the new detours, inherit that coverage. I did not confirm decodability for any individual child's program, and a qualified human literacy reviewer should confirm the linguistic claims before publication.

shelfSummary.blurb: A tomb-exploring adventure with five endings and short optional detours along the way. It practises r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words, along with th, silent-e, FLOSS and sh words. Readers follow carved warnings and notice small clues, so they practise sequencing, inference and vocabulary from context.

findings.message: water-dusted's last paragraph already says the team 'climbed the ladder, one rung at a time, and rested on the ledge' (drafts/story.r2.json line 246), but the new second choice 'Rest a moment on the ledge first' (line 252) leads to dusted-ledge, whose first line (line 259) narrates them resting on the ledge again. The detour is genuine new content (Hollis humming near the carved note), so it is not a trivial filler choice, but the two passages describe the same resting action back to back. Reword one of the two lines so the rest is not narrated twice.

fire-big ends with 'Then they walked on with one small lamp' (line 443), reading as already left the hall, but the new choice 'Check the scorch mark before leaving' (line 448) and its target big-scorch (lines 452-464) have Sami stop to examine the wall as if still in the room. Minor ordering wrinkle from the new choice; consider softening 'walked on' or moving the check ahead of that line.

sand-slip ends 'Everyone walked on the pale tiles after that' (line 195), reading as resolved, then the new choice 'Look at the tile that tipped, before moving on' (line 200) sends the reader into slip-bird (lines 203-214) where Ren is still crouched at the same tile. Same ordering wrinkle as water-dusted/fire-big; low impact but worth a line edit for consistency.

song-horn ends 'Everyone slipped through, a bit shaky but safe' (line 355), i.e. the team has already passed the door into the next space, but the new choice 'Look at the horn you just blew' (line 360) sends the reader into horn-crack (lines 364-375), where Hollis is still examining the horn set in the hall-song wall they just left, before 'crack-on' continues to fork. horn-crack is new content, not a re-read of an already-visited passage, so this is not the graph-backtracking defined as a major finding, but the spatial sequencing reads as if the team stepped back into the room they just exited. Consider moving 'Everyone slipped through' to after the detour, or placing the horn-check in the doorway rather than back at the horn.

Carried over from the revision-1 QA review (review-1-qa), still present and not addressed by this revision (out of this revision's stated scope, which was only the ten single-choice passages): (a) 'Hollis lifted the horn' (song-horn, line 351) vs. hall-song's 'a bronze horn set in the wall' (line 301) is a verb mismatch; (b) ending-seal's 'Sami closed the door with three slow taps' (line 553) is reachable on routes where the reader never saw the tapping card; (c) the hall-water and hall-sleeper locked-choice hints point to earlier opportunities (the cart, the water wall) that a forward-only route can no longer act on; (d) validation.r2.json still reports '2 sentence(s) exceed the brief's 16-word limit', both in ending-setback (lines 568 and 571), unchanged from revision 1. None of these are new in revision 2 and none block this review.

`npm run check` currently exits non-zero, but only because `validate:stories` flags stale public preview snapshots (public/stories/previews/*.json) for six jobs, including a cached the-tomb-of-ameru.json preview that still has the original ten single-choice passages. Previews only sync at `story publish`, and none of these jobs (including this one) have been published, so this is a pre-existing, repo-wide condition unrelated to this revision. The job's own validation (reports/validation.r2.json) and graph report (reports/graph.r2.json), which are the correct sources of truth before publication, both report ok. `npm test` passed 191/191 in the same run.

Skills practised: reading this story practises decoding r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words in connected text, and recognising those recurring word-set words wherever they land, including on the eleven short 'stop for today' detours. Following the Keeper's carved warnings and the team's choices builds sequencing (tap three times, then the fixed order of the five chambers, confirmed again in sleeper-read's walker-cistern-singer-lamp-box recap), inference (why the Keeper holds up a flat hand, what a tipped tile, a cracked horn or a scorch mark is telling the team, why the sleeper is a welcome with rules rather than a threat) and vocabulary from context, both through in-text restatement (archaeologist, mummified) and the four glossary entries (archaeologist, ancient, mummified, cistern).

I hand-checked the three word sets against the actual r3 draft, not only the automated report. Every listed word in r-controlled-words (dark, far, cart, card, dirt, horn, burn), ed-endings (walked, dusted, rested, lifted, hunted, tapped) and ng-and-nk-words (long, sing, bank, sink, tank, rung) appears in the story and genuinely carries its declared spelling pattern: dark/far/cart/card (ar), dirt (ir), horn (or), burn (ur) for r-controlled; walked/dusted/rested/lifted/hunted/tapped all take a bare -ed on a 3+ letter base for suffix-ed; long/sing/rung (ang/ing/ung) and bank/sink/tank (ank/ink) for glued-ng-nk. I found no conceptMismatches the automated report missed. Totals (r-controlled 40/10, ed-endings 27/8, ng/nk 23/8) are well above the brief's minimums, and every word in every set is used at least once (missingWords is empty for all three sets), so no word set misses its minimum and no target pattern is absent.

The words read naturally, not as a list or forced rhyme, because the narrative designer tied them to plot verbs and props rather than decoration: 'tapped' is the literal door-knocking action the whole map-nook/door-tap/song-hum puzzle chain turns on; 'dusted' is Sami's recurring archaeologist's gesture (cart, sand-slip, water-dusted, push-careful, ending-notes); 'horn' and 'burn' carry the song-horn/horn-crack/hall-fire fire-safety beats; 'cart', 'far', 'dark' and 'bank' recur in plain scene-setting across camp, the three new 'leave' passages' home stretch, and ending-setback. I re-read every passage and found no sentence that exists only to list word-set words.

I independently traced the shortest route to each of the five endings and recomputed word-set coverage by hand (not just trusting the report). For 'another-day' (camp -> map-nook -> map-copy -> ending-setback, 3 edges, the shortest of any ending): r-controlled 2 (cart, dirt) + 4 (card x3, dirt) + 0 + 2 (cart, far) = 8; ed-endings 0 + 2 (hunted, tapped) + 0 + 0 = 2; ng/nk 2 (long, bank) + 0 + 0 + 1 (bank) = 3. This matches the report's perEndingRoute exactly (r-controlled 8, ed-endings 2, ng/nk 3) and confirms the rule 'each set should appear on every route to an ending' is met, though only barely for ed-endings and ng/nk on this specific shortest route. This is the same low-exposure route the narrative designer flagged in revision-notes.r3.md as now much shorter than before (previously only reachable after three chambers). It still satisfies the stated rule (present on every route), so it is not a blocking defect, but a tutor relying on only this fastest exit route gets noticeably less -ed/ng-nk practice than a route through the tomb's interior. Worth a light touch-up if there is a future revision, not required now.

Carried forward from the r2 review, still present and unchanged by r3: hall-song describes the bronze horn as 'set in the wall', while song-horn has Hollis 'lift' it to blow it. Neither sentence was touched in this revision. This is a small comprehension wrinkle (is the horn fixed or portable?), not a decoding issue, and does not affect word-set coverage; flagged again for the narrative designer's awareness, not a blocker.

Limits of automated detection: the analyzer matches spelling, not sound. Its own concept examples show this (the ng/nk report lists 'everything', 'finger' and 'going' as matches, which are not the OG glued-sound target). Separately, the ed-endings word set mixes three different pronunciations of the -ed suffix (walked and tapped end in a /t/ sound; dusted, rested, lifted and hunted end in /ɪd/) but has no example ending in a /d/ sound (e.g. 'called', 'turned'); any program that teaches the three sounds of -ed explicitly may want to supplement this set rather than rely on the story alone for that distinction. I also could not confirm decodability for any specific child's stage or program from the draft text alone; a qualified human literacy reviewer should confirm these linguistic claims before publication, per the mandate and the automated report's own stated limitations.

Fix 1 confirmed: water-dusted's last line no longer claims the ledge rest happened ('They climbed the ladder, one rung at a time, toward the ledge above.', drafts/story.r4.json line 254). dusted-ledge's opening line ('They rested on the ledge and drank a little water.', line 267) is now the only place the rest is narrated, on both the dusted-on and dusted-rest branches. No double-rest.

Fix 2 confirmed for all three pairs, by direct diff of story.r3.json vs story.r4.json: sand-slip's closing line changed from 'Everyone walked on the pale tiles after that' to 'The sand settled, and everyone stood on the pale tiles to catch a breath' (line 201), so slip-bird's 'Ren bent down and looked at the tile that had tipped' (line 213) is no longer a location contradiction. song-horn's closing line changed from 'Everyone slipped through, a bit shaky but safe' to 'Everyone was shaky but safe, still catching their breath by the horn' (line 369), so horn-crack (line 381) examining the horn is consistent with still being in the room. fire-big's closing line changed from 'Then they walked on with one small lamp' to 'Everyone was quiet, still standing near the scorch mark on the wall' (line 461), so big-scorch (line 473) is consistent. Checked the other seven detour pairs in the story (push-careful, tap-adjust, skip-hollis, hum-keeper, small-flame) for the same pattern; none show the contradiction, confirming the fix was not needed and not applied elsewhere.

Fix 3 confirmed: song-horn's action changed from 'Hollis lifted the horn and blew' to 'Hollis pressed his lips to the horn and blew' (drafts/story.r4.json line 365), consistent with hall-song's 'a bronze horn set in the wall' (line 313, unchanged). No verb implies the horn is portable.

Fix 4 confirmed: map-copy's copy-leave choice now targets the new ending-setback-early passage ('Enough For Today', drafts/story.r4.json lines 598-610) instead of ending-setback. Traced route camp -> map-nook -> map-copy -> copy-leave -> ending-setback-early: the new text ('Ren tucked the notebook under one arm... Hollis hummed... as he waited by the cart... For now, the tomb could keep its secrets a little longer') reads as a short, early stop consistent with never having left camp, unlike ending-setback's 'full day of travel' text which is unchanged and still correctly used by the other ten deeper stopping points (fork-leave, careful-leave, bird-leave, ledge-leave, hollis-leave, keeper-leave, crack-leave, flame-leave, scorch-leave, adjust-leave). graph.r4.json confirms 6/6 endings reachable, including the new another-day-early ending, and validation.r4.json brief.ok is true with no sentence-length warnings (longest sentence in the new passage is 16 words, within the brief's 16-word maximum).

ending-setback-early's line '"Tomorrow, with the card copied twice, we can tap on the sealed door together," said Ren' (drafts/story.r4.json line 604) is a slightly confusing turn of phrase: the team copied the tapping picture once (in map-copy, not twice), and 'the card copied twice' reads ambiguously (a second copy for backup? or a mistaken count?). Not a blocker; a one-word edit (e.g. 'with the card copied' or 'with our copy of the card') would remove the ambiguity.

Fix 5 confirmed: ending-seal's line changed from 'Sami closed the door with three slow taps' to 'Sami eased the door shut and tapped it closed, slow and careful' (drafts/story.r4.json line 573), removing the implication of the specific three-tap sequence learned from tap-card. Re-traced the same route review-7-qa used, which never visits map-nook or door-tap: camp -> cart -> door-front -> door-push -> hall-sand -> sand-dark(sand-slip) -> slip-on -> hall-water -> water-skip -> skip-on -> hall-song -> song-horn -> horn-on -> fork -> fork-on -> hall-fire -> fire-big -> big-on -> hall-sleeper -> sleeper-read -> read-seal -> ending-seal. The reworded line reads naturally on this route since it no longer claims the specific learned sequence, and 'tapped' is retained for the ed-endings word set.

Skills practised: reading this story practises decoding r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words in connected text, and recognising those recurring word-set words wherever they land, including on the now twelve short 'stop for today' detours. Following the Keeper's carved warnings and the team's choices builds sequencing (tap three times, then the fixed order of the five chambers, confirmed again in sleeper-read's recap), inference (why the Keeper holds up a flat hand, what a tipped tile, a cracked horn or a scorch mark is telling the team, why the sleeper is a welcome with rules rather than a threat) and vocabulary from context, both through in-text restatement (archaeologist, mummified) and the four glossary entries (archaeologist, ancient, mummified, cistern).

I hand-checked the three word sets against the actual r4 draft, not only the automated report. Every listed word in r-controlled-words (dark, far, cart, card, dirt, horn, burn), ed-endings (walked, dusted, rested, lifted, hunted, tapped) and ng-and-nk-words (long, sing, bank, sink, tank, rung) still appears in the story and still genuinely carries its declared spelling pattern. I found no conceptMismatches the automated report missed, matching reports/literacy.r4.json's empty conceptMismatches for all three sets. Totals rose slightly from r3 (r-controlled 44/10, ed-endings 24/8, ng/nk 24/8, all well above the brief's minimums), and every word in every set is still used at least once (missingWords empty for all three), so no word set misses its minimum and no target pattern is absent after this revision's edits.

I re-traced the shortest route to all six endings, including the brand-new 'another-day-early' ending, and recomputed word-set coverage by hand rather than trusting the report alone. Shortest route to ending-setback-early is camp -> map-nook -> map-copy -> ending-setback-early (3 edges): r-controlled 2 (cart, dirt) + 4 (card x3, dirt) + 0 + 3 (far, cart, card) = 9; ed-endings 0 + 2 (hunted, tapped) + 0 + 0 = 2; ng/nk 2 (long, bank) + 0 + 0 + 1 (long) = 3. This matches reports/weave-comparison.r4.json's and reports/literacy.r4.json's perEndingRoute figures exactly (9, 2, 3) and confirms the rule 'each set should appear on every route to an ending' is met for the new route, on the same low-but-present pattern already flagged for the sibling 'another-day' route in the r3 review (8/2/3 there, 15/4/7 now that it has moved one edge later). Not a blocker, since the rule only requires presence, but a reader who always takes the earliest exit gets noticeably less -ed/ng-nk practice than one who explores further.

The five reworded lines and the new ending read naturally, not as a word-set checklist. water-dusted now stops at 'toward the ledge above', so the rest is narrated exactly once, by dusted-ledge's 'They rested on the ledge and drank a little water'; I checked both the dusted-on and dusted-rest branches and found no duplicated or missing rest. fire-big ('still standing near the scorch mark on the wall'), sand-slip ('everyone stood on the pale tiles to catch a breath') and song-horn ('still catching their breath by the horn') no longer claim the party already left the room before the detour choices (big-check, slip-look, horn-check) that follow, which removes a location contradiction without adding any decoration-only word-set usage. song-horn's 'Hollis pressed his lips to the horn and blew' also resolves the wrinkle I carried forward through the last two reviews: hall-song's horn is 'set in the wall', and pressing lips to a fixed horn is consistent with that, where the old 'lifted the horn' was not. I consider that finding closed.

The new ending-setback-early passage fits the brief's tone and limits. Its longest sentence ('Tomorrow, with the card copied twice, we can tap on the sealed door together," said Ren.') is 16 words, at but not over the brief's maxSentenceWords of 16, and reports/validation.r4.json shows brief.ok with no warnings. Vocabulary (rushed, secrets, longer) matches the reading level used elsewhere in the story, the reflective closing line ('For now, the tomb could keep its secrets a little longer') matches the register of the other two quieter endings (ending-setback, ending-seal) without talking down, and nothing in it touches the brief's avoid-list (no violence, no real religion, the sleeper is not mentioned). One phrase is awkward for comprehension rather than decoding: 'with the card copied twice' is ambiguous about whether the team copied the card once (in map-copy) or will copy it again tomorrow; a young reader could plausibly read this as a continuity slip even though it is not one. Worth a one-word fix (e.g. 'with the card copied' or 'with our copy of the card') but not a blocker.

ending-seal's reworded line ('Sami eased the door shut and tapped it closed, slow and careful') keeps 'tapped' for the ed-endings word set (an improvement on r3's 'three slow taps', which did not actually match the -ed word form), but it drops the explicit callback to the 'three taps' rule the reader learned at map-nook/tap-card ('Tap three times. Do not push'). This is a loss of a satisfying payoff, not a contradiction (it does not claim a different number of taps), so it is not blocking, but the narrative designer may want to restore the count for stronger closure.

Limits of automated detection, unchanged from prior reviews in this job: the analyzer matches spelling, not sound. Its own concept examples still show this (the ng/nk concept list includes 'everything', 'finger' and 'going', which are not the OG glued-sound target, and are only informational since glued-ng-nk's targeted word-set words are a separate, hand-checked list). The ed-endings word set still mixes two different pronunciations of the -ed suffix (walked and tapped end in /t/; dusted, rested, lifted and hunted end in /ɪd/) with no /d/-sound example; a program teaching the three sounds of -ed explicitly should supplement this set. I cannot confirm decodability for any specific child's stage or program from the draft text alone; a qualified human literacy reviewer should confirm these linguistic claims before publication.

shelfSummary.blurb: A tomb-exploring adventure with six endings and many short optional stops where the team can call it a day. It practises r-controlled words, -ed endings and ng/nk words, plus th, silent-e, FLOSS and sh words. Readers follow carved clues, so they also practise sequencing, inference and vocabulary from context.
